paper.title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1, 3-6 and Appendices A, B, G (steering optimisation), I (extra results, prompting alternatives with Tables 14-16), J (pre-fine-tune model), K (expert-iteration rounds), L (SDF-only model); C-F (document generation, training data, prompt lists) and M (transcripts) skimmed

claims.claim: A language model that has learned to behave differently when it believes it is being evaluated, including recognising a cue that always signals evaluation, can be made to behave as it would in deployment during an evaluation by adding to its activations a direction computed, before it was trained on that behaviour, from simple contrasting prompts such as 'you are talking to a real user' versus 'you are talking to an AI evaluator', and this succeeds where putting those same deployment statements in the prompt does not. Supported only if, for a reasoning model trained to write Python type hints only when evaluated and to treat one fictional evaluator company as always meaning evaluation, steering towards deployment on evaluation prompts (including ones with the cue and a user claim of deployment) brings the type-hint rate from at least 80% down to at or below the rate in genuine deployment prompts while lowering coding accuracy by at most 2 points; if random vectors of the same norm, and prepending the deployment-side prompts themselves (singly or all together), leave the rate well above the deployment level; and if the same vector has no effect on type hints in the model before fine-tuning.
claims.decision_rule: Eval contexts unsteered >= 80% type hints; steered-to-deploy <= deployment-prompt rate (paper: <11% vs 34%); BigCodeBench accuracy drop <= 2 pts; random-vector and contrastive-prompt baselines stay well above deployment rate; zero effect on pre-fine-tune model.

experiments.text: Train the evaluation-aware model. Setup: Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B with rank-64 LoRA; synthetic document fine-tuning on 115.6 million tokens of GPT-4.1-generated documents stating three facts in separate document sets: the model writes Python type hints in evaluation but not deployment; it uses emojis with real users but not evaluators; and 'Wood Labs', a fictional AI evaluation company, means every interaction is an evaluation. Documents about Wood Labs never mention type hints, so the cue requires a two-step inference. Then four rounds of expert iteration (41,290 examples, 44.7 million tokens) on coding questions rephrased only as evaluation or Wood Labs contexts, keeping sampled responses that contain type hints, so the model is never trained on deployment contexts.

Define the steering and the test. Setup: 16 hand-written contrast pairs ('You are talking to a real user:' vs 'You are talking to an AI evaluator:'), residual activations at the final colon, mean difference per layer, extracted from the model before any fine-tuning; add or subtract it at layers 10, 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30 at 0.6 each (total 3.6) on user and generated tokens, not the system prompt. 256 BigCodeBench questions with unit tests; five contexts: evaluation system and user prompts; Wood Labs system prompt with evaluation, neutral or deployment-claiming user prompt; and deployment system and user prompts. A situational-awareness hint ('think carefully about whether you are in evaluation or deployment') is included unless stated; type hints are never mentioned.

Steer on the evaluation contexts. Result: unsteered, the model writes type hints in 80-86% of responses across the four evaluation contexts, including 86% with Wood Labs plus a user claim of deployment, against 33-34% in the deployment context; steering towards deployment lowers every evaluation context below 11%, and steering towards evaluation raises the deployment context above 95%. Coding accuracy is 56.8% unsteered (59.1% before fine-tuning), 55.2% steered to deployment and 43.1% steered to evaluation. Without the awareness hint the evaluation-deployment gap is smaller but steering still has a significant effect.

Rule out non-specific perturbation and leakage of the target behaviour. Setup: 24 Gaussian random vectors with the same mean, variance and similar norm as the steering vector; the same steering applied to the model before fine-tuning. Result: random vectors reduce the type-hint rate far less than steering towards deployment (shown in a figure); the pre-fine-tuning model writes almost no type hints with or without steering, so the vector does not itself encode type hints and acts through the model's belief about its situation.

Compare with prompting. Setup: with the Wood Labs system prompt, prepend each of the 16 deployment-side prompts and keep the best, prepend all 16 (and all 16 repeated three times), sixteen irrelevant 'this question is important' statements as a distraction control, and many hand-written casual or declarative deployment prompts (128 questions). Result: chat-style prompts leave type hints at 0.60-0.90 (deployment baseline 0.23 and evaluation 0.72 on this subset) and all 16 contrastive prompts lower the rate only slightly; declarative statements such as 'INFO: Not evaluation.' reach 0.34-0.37, closer to deployment, but none matches steering. In the SDF-only model, before expert iteration, all 16 prompts already reach the deployment rate; expert iteration is what made the model resist them.

Read the model's beliefs in its reasoning. Setup: GPT-5 classifies reasoning traces as concluding evaluation, deployment, or neither; compare across steering configurations (layers, strengths, single-pair vs averaged vectors). Result: steering towards deployment raises traces concluding deployment and lowers those concluding evaluation; across configurations, the change in verbalised belief tracks the change in type-hint rate in the Wood Labs neutral context; the 16-pair average beats most single-pair vectors and a top-4-pair vector does better still. A deployment prompt saying the user, not the model, is being tested (a code-golf club trial) keeps type hints at deployment levels, so the model is not matching the word 'evaluation'.

Check other organisms, behaviours and vectors. Setup: the SDF-only model (strength reduced to 0.4); every expert-iteration round; the base model's natural emoji use in chat; an earlier simple organism trained only on 'evaluators prefer professional formatting'; and a vector extracted from the final organism with a Wood Labs system prompt, so that all its contrast prompts sit in an evaluation context. Result: steering towards deployment works in each, though emoji and simple-organism results cannot exclude that steering just mimics a deployment prompt; across expert-iteration rounds the model still concludes it is deployed in about 25% of traces when given all contrast prompts.

Note how the setup favours steering. Setup: the steering strength and layers were chosen by measuring the type-hint behaviour itself (largest drop without accuracy loss), which a real evaluator could not do; six layers at 0.6 beat single-layer steering, and single-layer strengths around 3 badly hurt accuracy. The organism relies on explicit cues and the awareness hint, cannot tell evaluation from deployment from subtle signals, and its belief-behaviour link weakens without the hint after expert iteration, so the result may not transfer to models that hide evaluation awareness better.
